descriptionA: How you SELECT participants from a population. Every member has an equal chance of being chosen.
descriptionB: How you PLACE participants into groups (experimental vs control) once they're already in the study.
keyDifference: Sampling = selecting from population. Assignment = placing into groups.
examTip: AP exam frequently tests this distinction. Random sampling affects generalizability; random assignment affects causation.

descriptionA: Associating two stimuli together to produce an involuntary response (NS + UCS → CS → CR).
descriptionB: Associating a behavior with its consequences (reinforcement increases behavior; punishment decreases it).
keyDifference: Classical = stimulus-stimulus association. Operant = behavior-consequence association.
examTip: If the scenario involves a CONSEQUENCE following a BEHAVIOR, it's operant. If it involves PAIRING two stimuli, it's classical.

descriptionA: ADDING a desirable stimulus to INCREASE behavior. Example: giving a sticker for good work.
descriptionB: REMOVING an undesirable stimulus to INCREASE behavior. Example: turning off an annoying alarm when you get up.
keyDifference: Both INCREASE behavior. Positive = add something. Negative = remove something.
examTip: Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment. Both types of reinforcement increase behavior.

descriptionA: Getting used to an unchanging stimulus at the sensory level (neurons stop responding).
descriptionB: Learning from a repeated stimulus that results in decreased responsiveness (behavioral learning).
keyDifference: Adaptation is a sensory/neural process. Habituation is a learned behavioral response.
examTip: Adaptation: you stop smelling perfume after wearing it. Habituation: you stop noticing a ticking clock.

descriptionA: OLD memories interfere with ability to recall NEW information.
descriptionB: NEW memories interfere with ability to recall OLD information.
keyDifference: Proactive = old blocks new. Retroactive = new blocks old.
examTip: PRO = forward (old → new). RETRO = backward (new → old).

descriptionA: HOW BIG the effect is. Measures the magnitude of the relationship or difference (small ≈ 0.2, medium ≈ 0.5, large ≈ 0.8).
descriptionB: Whether the result is REAL (not due to chance). Typically p < 0.05.
keyDifference: Effect size = magnitude. Significance = probability results aren't from chance.
examTip: A study can be statistically significant but have a tiny effect size. These are SEPARATE concepts.

descriptionA: Changing behavior to match the GROUP without being directly told to.
descriptionB: Complying with direct ORDERS from an authority figure.
keyDifference: Conformity = peer pressure (indirect). Obedience = authority pressure (direct order).
examTip: Asch = conformity. Milgram = obedience.

descriptionA: Inability to recall memories formed BEFORE an event.
descriptionB: Inability to form NEW memories AFTER an event.
keyDifference: Retrograde = lose the past. Anterograde = can't make new memories.
examTip: RETRO = looking backward. ANTE = looking forward.

descriptionA: Biased THINKING about a group of people (attitude).
descriptionB: Biased ACTIONS against a group of people (behavior).
keyDifference: Prejudice = attitude/thought. Discrimination = action/behavior.
examTip: You can be prejudiced without discriminating, but discrimination typically stems from prejudice.

descriptionA: Participants must be told about the study and agree to participate. Used with adults.
descriptionB: Required when working with MINORS. Children agree to participate with simpler explanation.
keyDifference: Consent = adults. Assent = minors. Both are required but serve different populations.
examTip: Do NOT mix these up. The CED specifically distinguishes them.

descriptionA: Perception driven by external sensory information. The brain builds understanding from raw data without prior expectations.
descriptionB: Perception driven by prior knowledge, expectations, and experiences. The brain fills in gaps based on what it already knows.
keyDifference: Bottom-up = data-driven (stimulus → brain). Top-down = knowledge-driven (brain → interpretation).
examTip: Reading a text with typos and still understanding it is top-down. Analyzing an unfamiliar object feature by feature is bottom-up.

descriptionA: Consciously recalled information (declarative). Includes episodic (personal events) and semantic (general facts).
descriptionB: Information or skills learned without full awareness. Includes procedural memory (how to ride a bike, type on keyboard).
keyDifference: Explicit = conscious recall. Implicit = unconscious, automatic.
examTip: Remembering your birthday party = explicit (episodic). Riding a bike without thinking about it = implicit (procedural).

descriptionA: Retrieving information without cues, like answering a fill-in-the-blank question.
descriptionB: Identifying information when presented with cues, like answering a multiple-choice question where the answer is in front of you.
keyDifference: Recall = no cues (harder). Recognition = with cues (easier).
examTip: Fill-in-the-blank = recall. Multiple choice = recognition. This is why multiple choice often feels easier.

descriptionA: Measures what someone CURRENTLY knows at a specific point in time.
descriptionB: Predicts how well someone will PERFORM in the future.
keyDifference: Achievement = current knowledge (backward-looking). Aptitude = future performance (forward-looking).
examTip: A final exam = achievement test. The SAT predicting college success = aptitude test.

descriptionA: Studies people of DIFFERENT ages at the SAME point in time. Quicker and cheaper but risks cohort effects.
descriptionB: Follows the SAME group of people over an EXTENDED period of time. Clearer developmental picture but costly and time-consuming.
keyDifference: Cross-sectional = snapshot of different ages now. Longitudinal = same people tracked over years.
examTip: Cross-sectional risk: cohort effects (generational differences). Longitudinal risk: attrition (participants dropping out).

descriptionA: HIGH demands with LOW warmth. Strict rules with little flexibility or emotional responsiveness.
descriptionB: HIGH demands with HIGH warmth. Clear expectations combined with responsiveness and open communication.
keyDifference: AuthoritARIAN = rigid rules, no warmth. AuthoritATIVE = firm rules + warmth and support.
examTip: Easy to mix up due to similar names. Focus on warmth: authoritarian lacks it, authoritative has it. Cultural context matters for outcomes.

descriptionA: Explaining behavior based on INTERNAL qualities like personality, character, or intelligence.
descriptionB: Explaining behavior based on EXTERNAL circumstances like the situation or environment.
keyDifference: Dispositional = blame the person. Situational = blame the circumstances.
examTip: The fundamental attribution error is OVERUSING dispositional attributions for OTHER people's behavior while favoring situational ones for our own.

descriptionA: POSITIVE stress that motivates and enhances performance. Feels exciting or challenging.
descriptionB: NEGATIVE stress that overwhelms and impairs functioning. Feels threatening or unmanageable.
keyDifference: Eustress = good stress (motivating). Distress = bad stress (damaging).
examTip: Pre-game butterflies = eustress. Chronic work overload = distress. Not all stress is harmful.

descriptionA: SEVERE depressive symptoms lasting at least TWO WEEKS. Intense episodes that significantly impair functioning.
descriptionB: MILDER but CHRONIC depressive symptoms lasting at least TWO YEARS. Less severe but longer-lasting.
keyDifference: Major = severe but shorter minimum (2 weeks). Persistent = milder but chronic (2 years minimum).
examTip: Duration and severity are the key distinguishing factors. Major depression can be episodic; persistent is ongoing.

descriptionA: Focuses on identifying and changing maladaptive THOUGHT PATTERNS. Uses cognitive restructuring and addresses the cognitive triad.
descriptionB: Focuses on changing maladaptive BEHAVIORS using conditioning principles. Includes systematic desensitization, token economies, and biofeedback.
keyDifference: Cognitive = fix the thinking. Behavioral = fix the behavior. CBT combines both.
examTip: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) merges both approaches. DBT and REBT are specific types of CBT.

descriptionA: After learning an outcome, believing you 'knew it all along.' Looking BACKWARD and feeling the result was obvious.
descriptionB: Overestimating the accuracy of your current knowledge and future predictions. Being too certain RIGHT NOW.
keyDifference: Hindsight = backward-looking ('I knew it'). Overconfidence = forward-looking ('I'm sure I'm right').
examTip: Together, these two biases make us overestimate our intuition. Both undermine the need for scientific research.

descriptionA: Performing BETTER on easy tasks and WORSE on hard tasks when others are watching. Being observed increases arousal.
descriptionB: Contributing LESS effort when individual contributions are NOT identifiable within a group.
keyDifference: Facilitation = being watched → arousal affects performance. Loafing = being in a group → effort decreases.
examTip: Key distinction: facilitation is about being OBSERVED individually. Loafing is about being HIDDEN in a group.

descriptionA: LOSING IDENTITY in a group, leading to impulsive or antisocial behavior one wouldn't normally do. Mob mentality.
descriptionB: Putting in LESS EFFORT when individual contributions aren't tracked. Free-riding in group work.
keyDifference: Deindividuation = losing your IDENTITY (acting out). Social loafing = losing your EFFORT (slacking off).
examTip: Deindividuation leads to doing things you shouldn't. Social loafing leads to NOT doing things you should.

descriptionA: Group discussion makes the DOMINANT VIEW more EXTREME. Like-minded people push each other to more radical positions.
descriptionB: Desire for group HARMONY suppresses disagreement. People sacrifice their own views for consensus.
keyDifference: Polarization = views become MORE EXTREME. Groupthink = views become MORE UNIFORM (dissent suppressed).
examTip: Polarization: everyone agrees and gets MORE passionate. Groupthink: people who disagree stay SILENT.

descriptionA: Attributing OTHERS' bad behavior to their disposition and YOUR OWN bad behavior to the situation. Applies to negative outcomes for both self and others.
descriptionB: Attributing YOUR SUCCESSES to disposition (internal) and YOUR FAILURES to the situation (external). Self-focused only.
keyDifference: Actor-observer = how you judge self vs others. Self-serving = how you explain your own wins vs losses.
examTip: Actor-observer: 'They tripped because they're clumsy; I tripped because the floor was wet.' Self-serving: 'I aced the test because I'm smart; I failed because it was unfair.'

descriptionA: Going along with the group to FIT IN and avoid judgment, even when you know they're wrong.
descriptionB: Going along with the group because you believe they have BETTER INFORMATION than you.
keyDifference: Normative = 'I don't want to be different.' Informational = 'They must be right.'
examTip: Normative: following fashion trends. Informational: looking at what others ordered at a new restaurant because they might know what's good.
